name: A billing alert auto-fires a subscription workflow
object: Stripe Workflows, a no-code automation builder that watches for a billing event and runs a chain of actions without custom scripts
audience: platform and finance teams running usage-based billing who are tired of hand-rolling scripts for billing edge cases
message: This video tells platform teams that Stripe Workflows can catch a billing alert and resolve it end to end with zero custom code and zero disruption to the customer.

moments.what: a presenter on the Stripe Sessions stage walks a pre-built automation canvas: a trigger node for a billing alert, a retrieve-customer step, then a branch on whether a payment method is on file
moments.copy: Here's a workflow I've pre-built. It fires the moment a billing alert triggers.

moments.what: the canvas opens both branches of the condition: if a payment method exists, auto-create a subscription and charge the customer; if not, update the customer record first
moments.copy: If a payment method is already active, it automatically generates the invoice, charges the customer, and starts a subscription.

moments.what: cut to a terminal; the presenter runs a live load test against a fictional customer account to push its usage over the free limit, with a requests-per-second chart climbing on screen
moments.copy: Let's hit some usage from Heroki to see it all come together live.

moments.what: cut to the Stripe dashboard on the customer's record: a new paid subscription now shows as active with no manual steps taken
moments.copy: The usage alert fired, the workflow triggered, and we automatically created a subscription with a charge. No disruption, no delays.

cta: no spoken call to action; the demo is staged as self-proof, closing on the dashboard showing the automation already resolved the billing event end to end
why: Watching the same canvas fire for real, under a live load test, turns an abstract automation diagram into something the viewer trusts: the trigger, the branch, and the dashboard proof all happen in one unbroken take, which is more convincing than any claim about reliability.
